title: Protenix-Mini: Efficient Structure Predictor via Compact Architecture, Few-Step Diffusion and Switchable pLM
authors: Chengyue Gong, Xinshi Chen, Yuxuan Zhang, Yuxuan Song, Hao Zhou, Wenzhi Xiao
reason: Presents a recent (2025) optimization of structure prediction using diffusion and pLMs, pushing the edge of efficient inference/SOTA deployment.
summary: Protenix-Mini addresses the high computational cost of protein structure prediction by replacing multi-step diffusion sampling with a two-step ODE sampler, pruning redundant transformer blocks, and substituting MSA modules with an ESM module. This streamlined architecture significantly reduces model complexity and inference time while maintaining high-fidelity predictions. The model achieves these efficiencies with only a negligible 1% to 5% decrease in performance compared to the full-scale Protenix model.

title: Learning the Language of Protein Structure
authors:
Benoit Gaujac, J\'er\'emie Don\`a, Liviu Copoiu, Timothy Atkinson,
  Thomas Pierrot, Thomas D. Barrett
reason: Presents a recent (2024) SOTA-style approach using vector-quantized autoencoders and GPT for de novo protein structure generation.
summary: To bridge the gap between continuous 3D protein structures and discrete language modeling, researchers developed a vector-quantized autoencoder that tokenizes protein backbones into discrete codebooks of 4,096 to 64,000 tokens. The method achieves high-fidelity structural reconstructions with backbone RMSD values between 1–5 Å. Using these learned representations, a GPT-based model successfully generates novel, diverse, and designable protein structures.

title: A Latent Diffusion Model for Protein Structure Generation
authors:
Cong Fu, Keqiang Yan, Limei Wang, Wing Yee Au, Michael McThrow, Tao
  Komikado, Koji Maruhashi, Kanji Uchino, Xiaoning Qian, Shuiwang Ji
reason: Represents the current frontier of protein design using generative diffusion models in latent space to create novel structures.
summary: Designing novel proteins is computationally difficult due to the vast complexity of protein structure modeling spaces. This study proposes a latent diffusion model that uses an equivariant protein autoencoder to compress structures into a latent space, where an equivariant diffusion model then learns to generate new representations. The method effectively generates novel protein backbone structures with high designability and computational efficiency.

title:
PSP: Million-level Protein Sequence Dataset for Protein Structure
  Prediction
authors:
Sirui Liu, Jun Zhang, Haotian Chu, Min Wang, Boxin Xue, Ningxi Ni,
  Jialiang Yu, Yuhao Xie, Zhenyu Chen, Mengyun Chen, Yuan Liu, Piya Patra, Fan
  Xu, Jie Chen, Zidong Wang, Lijiang Yang, Fan Yu, Lei Chen, Yi Qin Gao
reason: Provides a large-scale dataset and benchmark for training SOTA models, supporting the infrastructure of the field rather than a new prediction method.
summary: Current AI-driven protein structure prediction is limited by a lack of large-scale, diverse datasets for model training. The researchers developed PSP, a million-level dataset containing 570,000 true structure sequences and 745,000 distilled sequences, totaling 25TB of data. Using this dataset and a provided training benchmark, their model achieved first place in the CAMEO structure prediction contest.

title: Commutative Algebra Learning for Protein Flexibility Analysis
authors: Honghao Zhang, Hongsong Feng
reason: Focuses on B-factor (flexibility) prediction rather than the primary task of structure prediction (folding) or de novo design.
summary: Predicting protein flexibility (B-factors) is difficult because it requires capturing complex, multiscale local atomic environments. The researchers developed CAL, a framework that uses commutative algebra to create localized algebraic descriptors at multiple spatial scales. This method improves prediction accuracy by 34.5% over the classical Gaussian network model (GNM) across a benchmark of 364 proteins.

title: Consistent Synthetic Sequences Unlock Structural Diversity in Fully Atomistic De Novo Protein Design
authors: Danny Reidenbach, Zhonglin Cao, Zuobai Zhang, Kieran Didi, Tomas Geffner, Guoqing Zhou, Jian Tang, Christian Dallago, Arash Vahdat, Emine Kucukbenli, Karsten Kreis
reason: Presents a new SOTA framework (Proteina Atomistica) for atomistic de novo protein design, directly addressing the 'design' part of the question.
summary: Existing synthetic protein datasets often contain mismatched sequence-structure pairs that degrade the performance of generative models. The researchers developed the Consistency Distilled Synthetic Protein Database by using ProteinMPNN and structure prediction models to ensure synthetic sequences are both experimentally favorable and foldable. Training on this aligned dataset improved the structural diversity of the La-Proteina model by 54% and the Proteina Atomistica framework by 73%.

title: Advances of Deep Learning in Protein Science: A Comprehensive Survey
authors:
Bozhen Hu, Cheng Tan, Lirong Wu, Jiangbin Zheng, Jun Xia, Zhangyang
  Gao, Zicheng Liu, Fandi Wu, Guijun Zhang, Stan Z. Li
reason: A comprehensive survey covering deep learning applications in protein structure prediction and engineering, directly addressing the question.
summary: This survey addresses the challenge of modeling complex protein sequences, structures, and functions to advance drug discovery and protein engineering. The authors review various deep learning architectures, including convolutional, recurrent, attention, and graph neural networks, and their specific applications in predicting protein interactions and structures. The paper provides a comprehensive overview of current technological advancements, existing limitations, and future research directions in the field.

title: Attention Is All You Need
authors:
Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion
  Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
reason: While the Transformer architecture is foundational to modern protein models (like AlphaFold), this paper is about NLP/translation.
summary: Existing sequence transduction models rely on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that are difficult to parallelize. The authors propose the Transformer, a new architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that eliminates recurrence and convolutions. The model achieved a state-of-the-art 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German translation and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French translation while requiring significantly less training time.

title: Convolutional Networks on Graphs for Learning Molecular Fingerprints
authors:
David Duvenaud, Dougal Maclaurin, Jorge Aguilera-Iparraguirre, Rafael
  G\'omez-Bombarelli, Timothy Hirzel, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Ryan P. Adams
reason: Focuses on molecular fingerprints for property prediction rather than the 3D structure prediction or design of proteins.
summary: This research addresses the limitation of fixed molecular fingerprints by introducing a convolutional neural network that operates directly on graph-structured molecular data. The method generalizes circular fingerprinting to allow for end-to-end learning of features tailored to specific chemical tasks. The resulting data-driven features demonstrate improved interpretability and superior predictive performance across various molecular property prediction tasks compared to standard methods.

title:
AtomNet: A Deep Convolutional Neural Network for Bioactivity Prediction
  in Structure-based Drug Discovery
authors: Izhar Wallach and Michael Dzamba and Abraham Heifets
reason: Focuses on bioactivity prediction (drug discovery) using protein structures, rather than the prediction or design of the protein structures themselves.
summary: AtomNet addresses the limitation of existing drug discovery models by applying deep convolutional neural networks to structure-based bioactivity prediction. The method uses local convolutional filters to model chemical interactions and hierarchical features within structural target information. AtomNet outperforms traditional docking approaches, achieving an AUC greater than 0.9 on 57.8% of targets in the DUDE benchmark.

title: Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry
authors:
Justin Gilmer, Samuel S. Schoenholz, Patrick F. Riley, Oriol Vinyals,
  George E. Dahl
reason: Focuses on molecular property prediction via MPNNs rather than protein structure prediction or design; related methodology but different domain.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of predicting molecular properties by unifying various existing neural network models into a single, flexible framework called Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs). The researchers implemented several novel variations of this framework to learn how information is exchanged between atoms in a molecular graph. The MPNN approach achieved state-of-the-art results on standard molecular property prediction benchmarks, establishing a new performance baseline for the field.

title: Evaluating Protein Transfer Learning with TAPE
authors:
Roshan Rao, Nicholas Bhattacharya, Neil Thomas, Yan Duan, Xi Chen,
  John Canny, Pieter Abbeel, and Yun S. Song
reason: Focuses on protein language modeling and representation learning (embeddings) rather than direct structure prediction or design.
summary: To address the lack of standardized evaluation in protein modeling, researchers introduced TAPE, a benchmark consisting of five biologically relevant semi-supervised learning tasks. They evaluated various protein representation learning methods, finding that self-supervised pretraining significantly improves performance, sometimes more than doubling it. However, in several instances, these neural models still underperform compared to state-of-the-art non-neural techniques.

title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
authors:
Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, Eric A. Weiss, Niru Maheswaranathan, Surya
  Ganguli
reason: This is the foundational paper for Diffusion Models. While diffusion is used in protein design, this paper is about general ML, not protein structure.
summary: Researchers addressed the difficulty of creating flexible yet computationally efficient models for complex data distributions. They developed a method inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics that systematically destroys data structure through a forward diffusion process and learns to reverse it to restore structure. This approach enables the creation of deep generative models that can rapidly sample, evaluate, and compute conditional probabilities across thousands of layers or time steps.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
authors: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel
reason: While diffusion models are used in protein design (e.g., RFdiffusion), this specific paper is about general image synthesis and not protein structures.
summary: Generating high-quality images is difficult for many latent variable models, so this paper proposes using diffusion probabilistic models inspired by nonequilibrium thermodynamics. The researchers trained these models using a weighted variational bound that connects diffusion processes to denoising score matching. This method achieved state-of-the-art results on the CIFAR10 dataset, reaching an Inception score of 9.46 and an FID score of 3.17.

title: Learning from Protein Structure with Geometric Vector Perceptrons
authors:
Bowen Jing, Stephan Eismann, Patricia Suriana, Raphael J.L. Townshend,
  Ron Dror
reason: Introduces GVP, a key architectural component for geometric reasoning in protein modeling, though not the SOTA for prediction itself.
summary: Current machine learning models for large biomolecules often fail to simultaneously leverage both the graph-based relationships and the 3D geometric properties of protein structures. The researchers introduced Geometric Vector Perceptrons (GVPs), a new layer that extends standard dense layers to operate on collections of Euclidean vectors within a graph neural network framework. This approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art graph-based and voxel-based methods in both protein model quality assessment and computational protein design.

title: U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation
authors: Olaf Ronneberger and Philipp Fischer and Thomas Brox
reason: While U-Net is a foundational architecture in medical imaging, it is not a protein structure prediction or design method.
summary: Deep learning for biomedical image segmentation typically requires massive amounts of annotated data, which is often unavailable. The authors propose the U-Net architecture, which uses a symmetric contracting and expanding path combined with heavy data augmentation to enable efficient training from very few images. The model outperformed previous sliding-window methods in the ISBI challenge and can segment a 512x512 image in less than one second on a GPU.

title:
SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling
  quantum interactions
authors:
Kristof T. Sch\"utt, Pieter-Jan Kindermans, Huziel E. Sauceda, Stefan
  Chmiela, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Klaus-Robert M\"uller
reason: Focuses on quantum chemistry and molecular energy modeling rather than protein structure prediction or design.
summary: SchNet addresses the challenge of modeling quantum interactions in molecules without relying on a fixed grid, which would lose essential spatial information. The researchers developed a continuous-filter convolutional neural network that models local correlations based on precise atomic positions to predict total energy and interatomic forces. The architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks for equilibrium molecules and molecular dynamics trajectories while ensuring rotationally invariant energy predictions.

title:
ProtTrans: Towards Cracking the Language of Life's Code Through
  Self-Supervised Deep Learning and High Performance Computing
authors:
Ahmed Elnaggar, Michael Heinzinger, Christian Dallago, Ghalia Rihawi,
  Yu Wang, Llion Jones, Tom Gibbs, Tamas Feher, Christoph Angerer, Martin
  Steinegger, Debsindhu Bhowmik, Burkhard Rost
reason: Introduced large-scale protein language models (ProtT5) that provide embeddings for structure/function tasks without MSA, a key modern approach.
summary: Researchers trained six large-scale protein language models (including BERT, XLNet, and ProtT5) on 393 billion amino acids using high-performance supercomputing. By using these self-supervised embeddings as inputs for downstream tasks, the models achieved high accuracies in predicting protein secondary structure (81%–87%), sub-cellular localization (81%), and solubility (91%). Notably, the ProtT5 model outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods in per-residue predictions without requiring expensive evolutionary database searches.

title: ProtVec: A Continuous Distributed Representation of Biological Sequences
authors: Ehsaneddin Asgari and Mohammad R.K. Mofrad
reason: Focuses on sequence embeddings (word2vec style) for classification/properties; not a SOTA method for 3D structure prediction or design.
summary: This research addresses the need for efficient feature extraction from biological sequences by introducing ProtVec, a method that represents proteins as single dense n-dimensional vectors using artificial neural networks. When tested on 324,018 Swiss-Prot sequences, the method achieved an average protein family classification accuracy of 93% ± 0.06%, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, the vectors enabled highly accurate protein disorder prediction, distinguishing FG-Nup sequences from structured proteins with 99.8% accuracy and DisProt sequences with 100.0% accuracy.

title: E(n) Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
authors: Victor Garcia Satorras, Emiel Hoogeboom, Max Welling
reason: Introduces equivariant GNNs which are foundational to many protein models, but the paper focuses on general graphs and molecular properties.
summary: Current equivariant graph neural networks are often computationally expensive due to the need for higher-order representations and are typically limited to 3D spaces. This paper introduces E(n)-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs), which achieve equivariance to rotations, translations, reflections, and permutations using only first-order representations. The method scales easily to higher dimensions and demonstrates competitive or superior performance in tasks such as molecular property prediction and dynamical systems modeling.

title:
Accurate De Novo Prediction of Protein Contact Map by Ultra-Deep
  Learning Model
authors: Sheng Wang, Siqi Sun, Zhen Li, Renyu Zhang and Jinbo Xu
reason: A key early deep learning approach for contact prediction that paved the way for modern structure prediction, though superseded by AlphaFold.
summary: Predicting protein contacts for sequences without many homologs remains a challenge for accurate *de novo* structure prediction. This paper introduces an ultra-deep neural network composed of two deep residual networks that integrates evolutionary coupling and sequence conservation to model complex inter-contact correlations. The method achieved a top L long-range prediction accuracy of 0.47 (compared to 0.21 for CCMpred and 0.30 for MetaPSICOV) and enabled successful *ab initio* folding (TMscore > 0.6) for 203 test proteins.

title: Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution
authors: Yang Song and Stefano Ermon
reason: This is the foundational paper for score-based generative modeling (diffusion). While relevant to protein design methods, it is a general ML paper, not specific
summary: This research addresses the difficulty of estimating data distribution gradients when data lies on low-dimensional manifolds by perturbing the data with varying levels of Gaussian noise. The authors use score matching to estimate these gradients across all noise levels and employ annealed Langevin dynamics to generate samples. The method achieves a state-of-the-art inception score of 8.87 on the CIFAR-10 dataset, performing comparably to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

title: Computational Protein Design with Deep Learning Neural Networks
authors: Jingxue Wang, Huali Cao, and John Z.H. Zhang, and Yifei Qi
reason: Represents an early deep learning approach to protein design, providing context for the evolution toward modern SOTA generative models.
summary: Designing proteins for specific structures and functions remains a significant challenge despite the increasing availability of structural data. This study developed a multi-layer deep learning neural network to predict the probability of the 20 natural amino acids at each residue position based on extracted structural properties. The best network achieved 38.3% accuracy, and using its predictions as restraints in Rosetta improved sequence identity by approximately 3% compared to previous methods.

title: ProGen: Language Modeling for Protein Generation
authors:
Ali Madani, Bryan McCann, Nikhil Naik, Nitish Shirish Keskar, Namrata
  Anand, Raphael R. Eguchi, Po-Ssu Huang, Richard Socher
reason: A key early example of using LLMs for protein design/generation, though AlphaFold/RoseTTAFold represent the SOTA for structure prediction.
summary: To address the challenge of protein engineering without relying on costly structural annotations, researchers trained ProGen, a 1.2B-parameter language model, on approximately 280 million protein sequences using taxonomic and functional tags. The model enables fine-grained control over protein generation by conditioning on specific keywords, resulting in high accuracy in primary sequence similarity, secondary structure, and conformational energy.

title:
Diffusion probabilistic modeling of protein backbones in 3D for the
  motif-scaffolding problem
authors:
Brian L. Trippe, Jason Yim, Doug Tischer, David Baker, Tamara
  Broderick, Regina Barzilay, Tommi Jaakkola
reason: Introduces a key diffusion-based method for protein backbone design (motif scaffolding), a major component of the design aspect of the question.
summary: Designing protein scaffolds to support functional motifs is difficult because current machine-learning methods struggle to produce diverse structures or scaffolds longer than 20 residues. The researchers developed SMCDiff, an E(3)-equivariant diffusion model that samples protein backbone structures conditioned on a specific motif. The method successfully generates diverse scaffolds up to 80 residues in length that align closely with AlphaFold2-predicted structures.

title: Learning protein sequence embeddings using information from structure
authors: Tristan Bepler and Bonnie Berger
reason: Introduces representation learning for structural information via embeddings, a key precursor to modern protein language models used in prediction.
summary: To address the difficulty of detecting structural similarity between highly diverged protein sequences, researchers developed a representation learning framework that maps amino acid sequences into vector embeddings encoding structural information. The method uses bidirectional LSTM models trained via a two-part feedback mechanism incorporating global structural similarity and pairwise residue contact maps, utilizing a novel soft symmetric alignment (SSA) to compare embeddings of different lengths. The resulting embeddings outperform existing sequence-based methods and top structure-based alignment tools in predicting structural similarity, while also improving state-of-the-art performance in transmembrane domain prediction.

title: Graph Attention Networks
authors:
Petar Veli\v{c}kovi\'c, Guillem Cucurull, Arantxa Casanova, Adriana
  Romero, Pietro Li\`o, Yoshua Bengio
reason: While GATs are used in structural biology, this is a general machine learning architecture paper, not a protein structure prediction method.
summary: Existing graph neural networks often struggle with limitations in spectral-based methods and the inability to handle inductive tasks where graph structures change. This paper introduces Graph Attention Networks (GATs), which use masked self-attentional layers to allow nodes to assign different weights to their neighbors without requiring costly matrix operations. The model achieved or matched state-of-the-art results across four major benchmarks, including the Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, and protein-protein interaction datasets.

title:
Design of metalloproteins and novel protein folds using variational
  autoencoders
authors: Joe G Greener, Lewis Moffat, David T Jones
reason: An early application of generative deep learning (VAEs) to protein design, representing the lineage leading to modern diffusion models.
summary: Researchers used variational autoencoders to design novel protein sequences by conditioning them on specific desired properties, such as metal-binding sites or unique structural topologies. The method successfully generated sequences for new protein folds and added copper and calcium binding sites to non-binding proteins without human intervention. One designed candidate structure was validated as stable through molecular dynamics simulations.

title: SE(3)-Transformers: 3D Roto-Translation Equivariant Attention Networks
authors: Fabian B. Fuchs, Daniel E. Worrall, Volker Fischer, Max Welling
reason: Introduces SE(3)-equivariance in transformers, a critical architectural primitive used in SOTA protein models like AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold.
summary: Standard self-attention mechanisms lack equivariance to 3D rotations and translations, which can lead to unstable performance when input data is transformed. The researchers developed the SE(3)-Transformer, a self-attention variant that guarantees equivariance under continuous 3D roto-translations for point clouds and graphs. The model outperformed both non-equivariant attention baselines and existing equivariant models without attention on the ScanObjectNN and QM9 datasets.

title:
ProteinNet: a standardized data set for machine learning of protein
  structure
authors: Mohammed AlQuraishi
reason: Provides a standardized dataset and evaluation framework critical for training and benchmarking the models that define the current SOTA.
summary: Machine learning for protein structure prediction currently lacks standardized datasets with high-quality evolutionary information and rigorous data splits that prevent training on proteins too similar to those in the test set. The researchers developed ProteinNet, a series of datasets that integrates sequence, structure, and multiple sequence alignments into machine-learning-ready formats. This resource provides standardized training and validation splits that emulate the difficulty of CASP experiments by using sensitive evolutionary metrics to ensure true independence between data sets.

title: Directional Message Passing for Molecular Graphs
authors: Johannes Gasteiger, Janek Gro{\ss}, Stephan G\"unnemann
reason: Focuses on predicting quantum mechanical properties of small molecules via GNNs, not protein structure prediction or design.
summary: Standard graph neural networks for molecules often fail to account for the spatial directions between atoms, which are critical for predicting quantum mechanical properties. The researchers developed DimeNet, a directional message passing scheme that embeds messages with directional information using spherical Bessel functions and spherical harmonics. This approach achieves rotationally equivariant representations and outperforms previous models by an average of 76% on the MD17 dataset and 31% on the QM9 dataset while using less than 25% of the parameters.

title: Protein Representation Learning by Geometric Structure Pretraining
authors:
Zuobai Zhang, Minghao Xu, Arian Jamasb, Vijil Chenthamarakshan,
  Aurelie Lozano, Payel Das, Jian Tang
reason: Focuses on geometric representation learning for protein properties; relevant to the structural understanding required for prediction/design.
summary: Current protein representation models primarily rely on large-scale sequence pretraining, which fails to fully leverage the critical functional information contained in 3D structures. The researchers developed a geometric graph encoder trained via multiview contrastive learning and self-prediction tasks using structural data. This method achieves performance that meets or exceeds state-of-the-art sequence-based models in protein function prediction and fold classification while requiring significantly less pretraining data.

title: Deep generative models of genetic variation capture mutation effects
authors: Adam J. Riesselman, John B. Ingraham, Debora S. Marks
reason: Focuses on predicting mutation effects via sequence evolution (DeepSequence) rather than 3D structure prediction or de novo design.
summary: Most models for predicting how genetic mutations affect molecular function rely on simple additive or pairwise interactions, failing to capture complex, higher-order dependencies. The researchers developed DeepSequence, a latent variable model that learns nonlinear dependencies from evolutionary sequence data without requiring experimental labels. This approach predicts mutation effects across various deep mutational scanning experiments significantly more accurately than existing site-independent or pairwise models.

title: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs
authors: William L. Hamilton, Rex Ying, Jure Leskovec
reason: Introduces GraphSAGE for graph embeddings; while applicable to protein graphs, it is a general ML method, not a protein structure prediction/design paper.
summary: Existing graph embedding methods are transductive, meaning they cannot generate representations for new nodes without retraining the entire model. To solve this, the researchers developed GraphSAGE, an inductive framework that learns a function to aggregate features from a node's local neighborhood rather than learning fixed embeddings for individual nodes. This approach outperformed existing baselines on three benchmarks, including classifying unseen nodes in citation and Reddit datasets and generalizing to entirely new protein-protein interaction graphs.

title: End-to-End Learning on 3D Protein Structure for Interface Prediction
authors: Raphael J. L. Townshend, Rishi Bedi, Patricia A. Suriana, Ron O. Dror
reason: Focuses on protein-protein interface prediction rather than the primary task of folding (structure prediction) or de novo design.
summary: Predicting which protein surfaces interact is a data-limited task that current methods struggle to solve accurately due to reliance on hand-crafted features. The researchers developed the Siamese Atomic Surfacelet Network (SASNet), an end-to-end learning model that uses only atomic spatial coordinates and identities, and trained it on a new, large-scale dataset called DIPS. SASNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on gold-standard data, even when trained on only 3% of the DIPS dataset.

title:
Fold2Seq: A Joint Sequence(1D)-Fold(3D) Embedding-based Generative Model
  for Protein Design
authors:
Yue Cao and Payel Das and Vijil Chenthamarakshan and Pin-Yu Chen and
  Igor Melnyk and Yang Shen
reason: A generative model for protein design (sequence-from-fold) that was SOTA at its time, though newer diffusion models now lead the field.
summary: Designing novel protein sequences for a specific 3D fold is difficult due to the complex relationship between sequence and structure. Fold2Seq addresses this by using a transformer-based framework that jointly learns sequence embeddings and fold embeddings derived from 3D voxel densities of secondary structural elements. The model demonstrates improved or comparable speed, coverage, and reliability compared to existing deep generative models and RosettaDesign, particularly when handling low-quality or incomplete input structures.

title:
DeepSF: deep convolutional neural network for mapping protein sequences
  to folds
authors: Jie Hou, Badri Adhikari, Jianlin Cheng
reason: An early deep learning approach to fold recognition; important historical context for the transition from alignment to DL-based prediction.
summary: Traditional protein fold recognition methods rely on sequence alignment to templates, which fails to directly model the relationship between a sequence and its structure. Researchers developed DeepSF, a 1D convolutional neural network that automatically extracts features from protein sequences to classify them into one of 1,195 known folds. The model achieved a classification accuracy of 80.4% on SCOP1.75 datasets and outperformed the HHSearch method by 14.5%–29.1% on template-free modeling targets.

title: Deep convolutional networks for quality assessment of protein folds
authors:
Georgy Derevyanko, Sergei Grudinin, Yoshua Bengio, and Guillaume
  Lamoureux
reason: Focuses on protein quality assessment (QA), a key component of the prediction pipeline, though not the primary SOTA prediction method itself.
summary: Current protein structure assessment methods rely on manually engineered structural features, which limits their ability to learn directly from raw data. This research implements deep convolutional networks that predict model quality using only raw three-dimensional atomic densities without any predefined feature tuning. The network performs on par with state-of-the-art algorithms, achieving a loss of 0.064 on the CASP11 dataset compared to the best existing method's loss of 0.063.

title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
authors:
Yaron Lipman, Ricky T. Q. Chen, Heli Ben-Hamu, Maximilian Nickel, Matt
  Le
reason: Discusses a general generative modeling paradigm (Flow Matching). While relevant to future protein design methods, it is not about protein structure.
summary: This paper introduces Flow Matching (FM), a simulation-free method for training Continuous Normalizing Flows by regressing vector fields of fixed conditional probability paths. By using Optimal Transport displacement interpolation instead of standard diffusion paths, the method enables more efficient training and sampling. On ImageNet, FM consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based methods in both likelihood and sample quality while allowing for fast generation using standard ODE solvers.

title: Machine learning-guided directed evolution for protein engineering
authors: Kevin K. Yang and Zachary Wu and Frances H. Arnold
reason: Focuses on sequence-function optimization via directed evolution rather than the structural prediction/design (folding/geometry) requested.
summary: Traditional directed evolution is often limited by the vastness of sequence space, making it difficult to optimize complex protein functions efficiently. This paper outlines a framework for using machine learning to build sequence-function models that predict how mutations affect protein performance without requiring detailed physical models. By learning from all measured variants, these ML methods accelerate the engineering process and enable the selection of improved sequences more effectively than traditional methods.

title:
Hierarchical, rotation-equivariant neural networks to select structural
  models of protein complexes
authors:
Stephan Eismann, Raphael J.L. Townshend, Nathaniel Thomas, Milind
  Jagota, Bowen Jing, Ron O. Dror
reason: Introduces equivariant neural networks for scoring protein complex models, a key component in the structural prediction pipeline.
summary: Predicting the correct structure of multi-protein complexes is difficult because traditional methods rely on pre-defined physical or statistical features. This research introduces a hierarchical, rotation-equivariant neural network that learns to identify accurate protein models directly from 3D atomic coordinates without prior assumptions. When integrated with existing scoring functions, the method significantly improves the ability to distinguish accurate structural models from incorrect ones.

title:
GeoDiff: a Geometric Diffusion Model for Molecular Conformation
  Generation
authors: Minkai Xu, Lantao Yu, Yang Song, Chence Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jian Tang
reason: Focuses on small molecule/cheminformatics conformation generation rather than protein structure prediction or design.
summary: Predicting stable 3D molecular conformations from 2D molecular graphs is a core challenge in drug discovery. The researchers developed GeoDiff, a geometric diffusion model that treats atoms as particles and learns to reverse a noise-to-conformation process using equivariant Markov kernels to ensure roto-translational invariance. Experiments demonstrate that GeoDiff performs as well as or better than current state-of-the-art methods, showing particular strength in generating conformations for large molecules.

title: EquiBind: Geometric Deep Learning for Drug Binding Structure Prediction
authors:
Hannes St\"ark, Octavian-Eugen Ganea, Lagnajit Pattanaik, Regina
  Barzilay, Tommi Jaakkola
reason: Focuses on protein-ligand docking/binding rather than the primary task of protein structure prediction (folding) or de novo design.
summary: Predicting how drug-like molecules bind to protein targets is currently a slow process due to the heavy computational cost of sampling and scoring candidate poses. EquiBind uses an SE(3)-equivariant geometric deep learning model to directly predict both the binding location and the ligand's orientation in a single step. This method achieves significant speed-ups and higher prediction quality compared to traditional docking baselines.

title:
TopologyNet: Topology based deep convolutional neural networks for
  biomolecular property predictions
authors: Zixuan Cang and Guo-Wei Wei
reason: Focuses on property prediction (binding affinity, stability) using topological features rather than the core task of structure prediction or design.
summary: Predicting biomolecular properties is difficult because 3D structural data contains complex, entangled geometric and biological information. The researchers developed TopologyNet, which uses element-specific persistent homology (ESPH) to convert 3D geometry into 1D topological invariants represented as multichannel images for processing by convolutional neural networks. This approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in predicting protein-ligand binding affinities and the impacts of mutations on both globular and membrane proteins.

title: DiffDock: Diffusion Steps, Twists, and Turns for Molecular Docking
authors:
Gabriele Corso, Hannes St\"ark, Bowen Jing, Regina Barzilay, Tommi
  Jaakkola
reason: Focuses on molecular docking (ligand-protein binding) rather than protein structure prediction or de novo protein design itself.
summary: Current molecular docking methods struggle to improve accuracy over traditional search-based approaches. DiffDock addresses this by framing docking as a generative modeling problem, using a diffusion process over the degrees of freedom (translation, rotation, and torsion) of a ligand's pose. The model achieves a 38% top-1 success rate on the PDBBind dataset, significantly outperforming both traditional (23%) and previous deep learning (20%) methods.

title: SE(3)-Stochastic Flow Matching for Protein Backbone Generation
authors:
Avishek Joey Bose, Tara Akhound-Sadegh, Guillaume Huguet, Kilian
  Fatras, Jarrid Rector-Brooks, Cheng-Hao Liu, Andrei Cristian Nica, Maksym
  Korablyov, Michael Bronstein, and Alexander Tong
reason: Presents a novel generative paradigm (flow matching on SE(3)) for protein backbone design, representing the current cutting edge of the field.
summary: Generating novel protein structures is challenging due to the complex 3D rigid motions required to model backbones. The researchers developed FoldFlow, a series of generative models that use stochastic flow matching and Riemannian optimal transport to learn continuous-time dynamics over the SE(3) group. The models are faster and more stable to train than diffusion-based methods, successfully generating high-quality, diverse, and novel protein backbones of up to 300 amino acids.

title:
Independent SE(3)-Equivariant Models for End-to-End Rigid Protein
  Docking
authors:
Octavian-Eugen Ganea, Xinyuan Huang, Charlotte Bunne, Yatao Bian,
  Regina Barzilay, Tommi Jaakkola, Andreas Krause
reason: Focuses on rigid protein-protein docking (pose prediction) rather than the primary task of de novo structure prediction or protein design.
summary: This research addresses the problem of rigid-body protein-protein docking, which involves predicting the 3D relative orientation of two proteins. The authors developed EquiDock, an SE(3)-equivariant graph matching network that uses keypoint matching and a differentiable Kabsch algorithm to predict rotation and translation. The model achieves significant speed improvements and often outperforms existing docking software without requiring heavy candidate sampling or structural refinement.

title:
Protein secondary structure prediction using deep convolutional neural
  fields
authors: Sheng Wang, Jian Peng, Jianzhu Ma and Jinbo Xu
reason: A significant early deep learning approach for secondary structure prediction, though superseded by modern end-to-end folding models.
summary: Predicting protein secondary structure from sequence information has seen stagnant accuracy levels for nearly a decade. The researchers developed DeepCNF, a deep learning framework that combines hierarchical convolutional neural networks with conditional random fields to model both complex sequence-structure relationships and dependencies between adjacent labels. This method achieved a Q3 accuracy of ~84% and a Q8 accuracy of ~72% on CASP and CAMEO test proteins, significantly outperforming previous predictors.

title: Torsional Diffusion for Molecular Conformer Generation
authors:
Bowen Jing, Gabriele Corso, Jeffrey Chang, Regina Barzilay, Tommi
  Jaakkola
reason: Focuses on small molecule conformer generation (torsion angles) rather than protein structure prediction or de novo protein design.
summary: Current machine learning models for molecular conformer generation struggle to outperform traditional cheminformatics methods. This research introduces "torsional diffusion," a framework that operates on a hypertorus to model torsion angles using an extrinsic-to-intrinsic score model. The method produces superior conformer ensembles in terms of RMSD and chemical properties while operating orders of magnitude faster than previous diffusion-based models.

title:
Tranception: protein fitness prediction with autoregressive transformers
  and inference-time retrieval
authors:
Pascal Notin, Mafalda Dias, Jonathan Frazer, Javier Marchena-Hurtado,
  Aidan Gomez, Debora S. Marks, Yarin Gal
reason: Focuses on protein fitness prediction (variant effect) rather than structure prediction/design, but is a SOTA method in related sequence modeling.
summary: Predicting how protein mutations affect fitness is currently limited by the need for deep, high-quality sequence alignments. The researchers developed Tranception, a transformer architecture that uses autoregressive modeling combined with the retrieval of homologous sequences during inference. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating superior accuracy in predicting multiple mutations and scoring insertions/deletions compared to existing models.

title: Fast Graph Representation Learning with PyTorch Geometric
authors: Matthias Fey, Jan Eric Lenssen
reason: A general-purpose graph neural network library. While used in protein modeling, it is a tool rather than a protein-specific method.
summary: PyTorch Geometric addresses the challenge of efficiently performing deep learning on irregularly structured data like graphs, point clouds, and manifolds. The library implements a wide range of relational and 3D learning methods using specialized CUDA kernels and efficient mini-batching for varying input sizes. This approach achieves high data throughput and provides a standardized framework for comparative studies across diverse graph-based tasks.

title: Protein-Ligand Scoring with Convolutional Neural Networks
authors:
Matthew Ragoza (1), Joshua Hochuli (1), Elisa Idrobo (2), Jocelyn

reason: Focuses on protein-ligand scoring/binding affinity rather than the primary task of protein structure prediction or de novo design.
summary: Researchers developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) scoring function that uses 3D representations of protein-ligand interactions to automatically learn features correlating with binding affinity. The model was trained to distinguish between correct and incorrect binding poses as well as between known binders and non-binders. The resulting CNN scoring function outperformed the industry-standard AutoDock Vina in both pose prediction and virtual screening tasks.

title:
BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language
  Models
authors:
Jesse Vig, Ali Madani, Lav R. Varshney, Caiming Xiong, Richard Socher,
  Nazneen Fatema Rajani
reason: Focuses on interpretability of protein language models via attention mechanisms rather than the SOTA methods for structure prediction/design.
summary: This research addresses the lack of interpretability in protein Transformer models by applying "BERTology" methods to analyze their attention mechanisms. By examining three different architectures across two datasets, the study demonstrates that attention patterns successfully capture 3D folding structures, identify functional binding sites, and focus on increasingly complex biophysical properties as layer depth increases.

title:
HelixFold-Single: MSA-free Protein Structure Prediction by Using Protein
  Language Model as an Alternative
authors:
Xiaomin Fang, Fan Wang, Lihang Liu, Jingzhou He, Dayong Lin, Yingfei
  Xiang, Xiaonan Zhang, Hua Wu, Hui Li, Le Song
reason: Represents a significant direction in SOTA: moving from MSA-dependent models to faster, MSA-free prediction using protein language models.
summary: Traditional protein structure prediction methods like AlphaFold2 are slow because they rely on time-consuming Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) searches. The model achieves competitive accuracy with MSA-based methods on targets with large homologous families while significantly reducing prediction time.

title:
Deep Supervised and Convolutional Generative Stochastic Network for
  Protein Secondary Structure Prediction
authors: Jian Zhou and Olga G. Troyanskaya
reason: Focuses on secondary structure prediction using deep learning, a precursor to modern end-to-end folding, but predates current SOTA (AlphaFold/RoseTTAFold).
summary: Predicting protein secondary structure is a fundamental challenge due to the complexity of amino acid sequences. The researchers developed a supervised convolutional generative stochastic network (GSN) that uses deep hierarchical representations and a Markov chain to model conditional distributions. This method achieved a 66.4% Q8 accuracy on the CB513 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art performance of 64.9%.

title: AlphaFold Meets Flow Matching for Generating Protein Ensembles
authors: Bowen Jing, Bonnie Berger, Tommi Jaakkola
reason: Represents the current edge of the field by moving from static structure prediction to generative modeling of dynamic protein ensembles.
summary: To capture the dynamic structural ensembles necessary for protein function, researchers developed AlphaFlow and ESMFlow by fine-tuning single-state predictors like AlphaFold and ESMFold using a flow-matching generative framework. The method outperforms AlphaFold with MSA subsampling in balancing structural precision and diversity, and it accurately reproduces conformational flexibility and positional distributions from all-atom molecular dynamics. Additionally, the model can diversify static structures and converge to equilibrium properties faster than traditional physics-based MD simulations.

title: Equivariant Diffusion for Molecule Generation in 3D
authors: Emiel Hoogeboom, Victor Garcia Satorras, Cl\'ement Vignac, Max Welling
reason: Focuses on small molecule generation rather than protein structure prediction or protein design; related methodology but different scale/domain.
summary: This research addresses the challenge of generating 3D molecular structures by introducing an E(3) equivariant diffusion model that jointly processes atom coordinates and types. The method utilizes an equivariant denoising network to ensure the model remains consistent under Euclidean transformations. Experimental results show that this approach significantly outperforms previous 3D generative methods in both sample quality and training efficiency.

title:
Structure-aware Interactive Graph Neural Networks for the Prediction of
  Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
authors:
Shuangli Li, Jingbo Zhou, Tong Xu, Liang Huang, Fan Wang, Haoyi Xiong,
  Weili Huang, Dejing Dou, Hui Xiong
reason: Focuses on protein-ligand binding affinity prediction rather than the folding/structure prediction or de novo design of the protein itself.
summary: Current graph neural networks for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction often fail to fully utilize 3D biomolecular structural information and long-range atomic interactions. The researchers developed Structure-aware Interactive Graph Neural Networks (SIGN), which uses polar-inspired graph attention layers to preserve distance and angle information and pairwise interactive pooling to capture global interactions. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that SIGN outperforms existing models in predicting binding affinity.

title: Deep Learning in Protein Structural Modeling and Design
authors: Wenhao Gao, Sai Pooja Mahajan, Jeremias Sulam, and Jeffrey J. Gray
reason: A review paper summarizing deep learning applications in protein modeling and design, providing context for the field's evolution.
summary: This review examines how deep learning techniques are being applied to protein structural modeling and design, specifically addressing the challenges of predicting structures from sequences and engineering proteins for new functions. The authors categorize emerging computational approaches and analyze the transition from sequence to structure to function. The paper serves as a guide to bridge the gap between computational biology and computer science by highlighting current advancements and remaining hurdles in the field.

title: Distance-based Protein Folding Powered by Deep Learning
authors: Jinbo Xu
reason: A key precursor to modern end-to-end distance-based prediction methods, though superseded by AlphaFold2/3 for SOTA.
summary: To overcome the limitations of contact-based prediction and the need for time-consuming folding simulations, researchers developed a deep learning method to predict protein distance matrices that can be converted directly into 3D models using distance geometry. The method successfully folded 21 of 37 CASP12 hard targets within 4 hours on a standard Linux computer, outperforming direct coupling analysis (DCA) which could not fold any targets without simulation. Further validation on CASP13 and CAMEO targets demonstrated the model's ability to predict correct folds for new protein structures even when sequence homologs are limited.

title:
Atomic Convolutional Networks for Predicting Protein-Ligand Binding
  Affinity
authors: Joseph Gomes, Bharath Ramsundar, Evan N. Feinberg, Vijay S. Pande
reason: Focuses on protein-ligand binding affinity prediction (drug discovery) rather than the folding/structure prediction or design itself.
summary: Current drug discovery models rely on hand-tuned physical or chemical parameters to predict how well a drug molecule binds to a protein. This research introduces an atomic convolutional neural network that uses 3D spatial convolutions to learn chemical interactions directly from atomic coordinates. The model performs competitively with or outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods when predicting binding free energy on the PDBBind dataset.

title: Fast protein backbone generation with SE(3) flow matching
authors:
Jason Yim, Andrew Campbell, Andrew Y. K. Foong, Michael Gastegger,

title:
Intrinsic-Extrinsic Convolution and Pooling for Learning on 3D Protein
  Structures
authors:

title:
Iterative Refinement Graph Neural Network for Antibody
  Sequence-Structure Co-design
authors: Wengong Jin, Jeremy Wohlwend, Regina Barzilay, Tommi Jaakkola
reason: Focuses on the specific sub-task of antibody co-design (sequence and structure), representing a specialized application of the broader field.
summary: Designing effective antibodies requires optimizing both their amino acid sequences and their 3D structures simultaneously, rather than assuming a fixed structure beforehand. This paper introduces a generative model that autoregressively produces sequences while iteratively refining their predicted 3D structures as graphs. The method achieves superior log-likelihood on test sets and outperforms existing baselines in designing antibodies capable of neutralizing the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

title:

This method enables the model to learn more complex atomic environments, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while requiring up to three orders of magnitude less training data than existing models.

title: PiFold: Toward effective and efficient protein inverse folding
authors: Zhangyang Gao, Cheng Tan, Pablo Chac\'on, Stan Z. Li
reason: Focuses on protein design (inverse folding), a key part of the question. It presents a high-efficiency method, though not the absolute SOTA.
summary: Current protein inverse folding methods struggle to balance design accuracy with computational speed due to limited feature representation and slow autoregressive decoding. PiFold addresses this by using a novel residue featurizer and PiGNN layers to generate protein sequences in a single step. The method achieves a 51.66% recovery rate on the CATH 4.2 dataset while performing inference 70 times faster than existing autoregressive models.

title:
Out of Many, One: Designing and Scaffolding Proteins at the Scale of the
  Structural Universe with Genie 2
authors: Yeqing Lin, Minji Lee, Zhao Zhang, Mohammed AlQuraishi
reason: Directly addresses the state-of-the-art in protein design, claiming SOTA performance in designability, diversity, and motif scaffolding.
summary: Current protein diffusion models struggle to capture the full diversity of the structural universe and lack the ability to design complex, multi-functional proteins with multiple interacting motifs. The researchers developed Genie 2, an improved diffusion model featuring architectural innovations and a multi-motif framework that allows for the design of co-occurring motifs with unspecified relative orientations. Genie 2 achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods in designability, diversity, and novelty, while solving more motif scaffolding problems with a wider variety of unique solutions.

title: ProGen2: Exploring the Boundaries of Protein Language Models
authors:
Erik Nijkamp, Jeffrey Ruffolo, Eli N. Weinstein, Nikhil Naik, Ali
  Madani
reason: Represents a state-of-the-art approach in protein design via large-scale language models, though focused on sequence generation rather than structure.
summary: Researchers investigated how scaling model size and training data affects the performance of protein language models. They developed ProGen2, a suite of models scaled up to 6.4 billion parameters and trained on datasets containing over one billion protein sequences. The models achieved state-of-the-art results in capturing evolutionary distributions, generating viable novel sequences, and predicting protein fitness without additional fine-tuning.

title:
MUST-CNN: A Multilayer Shift-and-Stitch Deep Convolutional Architecture
  for Sequence-based Protein Structure Prediction
authors: Zeming Lin, Jack Lanchantin, Yanjun Qi
reason: A significant early deep learning approach for sequence-based property prediction, though superseded by transformer/diffusion models.
summary: Predicting protein properties like solvent accessibility and secondary structure from amino acid sequences is often limited by the efficiency of traditional window-based models. The researchers developed MUST-CNN, a deep convolutional architecture that utilizes a novel multilayer shift-and-stitch technique to generate dense, per-position predictions. This method outperformed existing state-of-the-art models on two large protein property prediction datasets while maintaining faster prediction speeds and a simpler architecture.

title:
Deep Learning of High-Order Interactions for Protein Interface
  Prediction
authors: Yi Liu, Hao Yuan, Lei Cai and Shuiwang Ji
reason: Focuses on protein-protein interface prediction rather than the primary task of folding (structure prediction) or de novo design.
summary: Existing protein interface prediction methods often fail to account for sequential amino acid information and high-order interactions between multiple residue pairs. This study proposes a deep learning model that represents proteins as graphs, incorporates sequential modeling, and uses a 3D tensor to capture high-order pairwise interactions for 2D dense prediction. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that this approach consistently improves prediction performance compared to previous methods.

title: ATOM3D: Tasks On Molecules in Three Dimensions
authors:
Raphael J.L. Townshend, Martin V\"ogele, Patricia Suriana, Alexander
  Derry, Alexander Powers, Yianni Laloudakis, Sidhika Balachandar, Bowen Jing,
  Brandon Anderson, Stephan Eismann, Risi Kondor, Russ B. Altman, Ron O. Dror
reason: Provides a benchmark and toolkit for 3D molecular learning, relevant to the infrastructure used for structure prediction/design tasks.
summary: The lack of standardized benchmarks and unified toolkits has hindered the adoption of 3D deep learning in biomolecular research. The researchers developed ATOM3D, a collection of benchmark datasets and an open-source Python package designed to evaluate various 3D molecular learning methods. Their results demonstrate that 3D-based models consistently outperform 1D and 2D representations, with specific architectures like equivariant and convolutional networks excelling depending on the task's geometric complexity.

title: Proteina: Scaling Flow-based Protein Structure Generative Models
authors:
Tomas Geffner, Kieran Didi, Zuobai Zhang, Danny Reidenbach, Zhonglin
  Cao, Jason Yim, Mario Geiger, Christian Dallago, Emine Kucukbenli, Arash

reason: Presents a new SOTA generative model (Proteina) for de novo protein design with scaling improvements and novel conditioning methods.
summary: Proteina addresses the limitations of current generative models in designing long, diverse, and controllable protein backbones. The researchers developed a scalable transformer-based flow model that utilizes hierarchical fold class labels for conditioning and can be trained on millions of synthetic structures. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in de novo design, producing designable proteins at unprecedented lengths of up to 800 residues.

title: La-Proteina: Atomistic Protein Generation via Partially Latent Flow Matching
authors: Tomas Geffner, Kieran Didi, Zhonglin Cao, Danny Reidenbach, Zuobai Zhang, Christian Dallago, Emine Kucukbenli, Karsten Kreis, Arash Vahdat
reason: Presents a new SOTA method (La-Proteina) for atomistic protein design using flow matching, directly addressing the current leading edge.
summary: Generating fully atomistic protein structures alongside their amino acid sequences is difficult because side-chain lengths vary, making explicit modeling complex. La-Proteina addresses this by using a partially latent representation that explicitly models the coarse backbone while capturing sequence and atomistic details through fixed-dimensional latent variables via flow matching. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in co-designability and structural validity, successfully generating valid proteins up to 800 residues in length where previous models fail.

title: Relaxed Sequence Sampling for Diverse Protein Design
authors: Joohwan Ko, Aristofanis Rontogiannis, Yih-En Andrew Ban, Axel Elaldi, Nicholas Franklin
reason: Presents a new MCMC framework (RSS) for protein design, improving diversity and designability, representing the current edge of design methods.
summary: Current protein design methods like relaxed sequence optimization (RSO) often fail to produce diverse or designable sequences because they rely on single-path gradient descent. This paper introduces Relaxed Sequence Sampling (RSS), an MCMC framework that combines gradient-guided exploration with protein language model-informed jumps to balance structural accuracy and evolutionary plausibility. In binder design tasks, RSS produces 5$\times$ more designable structures and 2-3$\times$ greater structural diversity than RSO baselines at the same computational cost.

title: Diffusion Language Models Are Versatile Protein Learners
authors:
Xinyou Wang, Zaixiang Zheng, Fei Ye, Dongyu Xue, Shujian Huang,

reason: Represents the current frontier by combining diffusion models with protein language modeling for both sequence generation and structure-conditioned design.
summary: Researchers developed Diffusion Protein Language Models (DPLM) by pre-training a discrete diffusion probabilistic framework on evolutionary-scale protein sequences. This method enables the model to perform both unconditional generation of novel, structurally plausible sequences and conditional tasks like inverse folding and motif scaffolding. The resulting model outperforms ESM2 in representation learning and can steer sequence generation toward specific properties, such as secondary structures, using classifier guidance.

title: Protein Design with Dynamic Protein Vocabulary
authors: Nuowei Liu, Jiahao Kuang, Yanting Liu, Tao Ji, Changzhi Sun, Man Lan, Yuanbin Wu
reason: Presents a novel generative design method (ProDVa) that improves structural plausibility and foldability, representing the current edge of design.
summary: Current text-to-protein generative models often struggle to design sequences that are structurally plausible and capable of folding correctly. The researchers developed ProDVa, a method that integrates a text encoder with a protein language model and a fragment encoder to dynamically retrieve natural protein fragments based on functional descriptions. ProDVa achieves comparable functional alignment using less than 0.04% of the training data while increasing the proportion of well-folded proteins (pLDDT > 70) by 7.38% and those with low PAE (< 10) by 9.6%.

title: Protein Design with Guided Discrete Diffusion
authors:
Nate Gruver, Samuel Stanton, Nathan C. Frey, Tim G. J. Rudner, Isidro

reason: Presents a novel guidance method (NOS) for discrete diffusion in sequence space, pushing the state-of-the-art in protein design capabilities.
summary: Current protein design methods often rely on complex structure-based models that suffer from data scarcity and difficult inverse design. This paper introduces NOS (diffusioN Optimized Sampling), a guidance method that allows for direct design in sequence space by following gradients within a discrete diffusion model's hidden states. When applied to antibody optimization, the resulting LaMBO-2 method achieved a 99% expression rate and a 40% binding rate in experimental tests.

title:
Generative Flows on Discrete State-Spaces: Enabling Multimodal Flows

authors:
Andrew Campbell, Jason Yim, Regina Barzilay, Tom Rainforth, Tommi

summary: Current generative models struggle to simultaneously process discrete and continuous data, such as protein sequences and structures. The researchers developed Discrete Flow Models (DFMs) using Continuous Time Markov Chains to bridge this gap, allowing for a unified flow-based framework. This method achieves state-of-the-art performance in protein co-design, enabling the flexible, joint generation of both protein sequences and 3D structures.

title: Transformers in Protein: A Survey
authors: Xiaowen Ling and Zhiqiang Li and Yanbin Wang and Zhuhong You
reason: Provides a comprehensive review of Transformer applications in protein structure prediction, covering recent advancements and datasets.
summary: This survey addresses the lack of a comprehensive overview regarding the application of Transformer architectures in protein informatics. The authors systematically review over 100 studies across domains such as structure prediction, function prediction, and drug discovery, while categorizing model variants and curating essential datasets. The paper provides a consolidated foundation for the field by identifying current limitations and proposing future research directions for integrating deep learning with protein science.
